objectives: Build a maintenance plan around fleet goals
body: At the expert level, the question shifts from "how do I fix this truck?" to "how do I keep the fleet available at the right cost?"

tiles.title: Reliability
tiles.text: How rarely equipment fails in service. Measured with metrics like breakdown frequency and MTBF.

tiles.title: Availability
tiles.text: Share of time equipment is ready to work. Reduced by every hour of downtime — planned or not.

tiles.title: Cost
tiles.text: Total maintenance spend and cost per mile, including the hidden costs of failures.

head: Strategy
Approach
Strength
Limitation
rows: May service too early or too late
Service when inspections or data show need (e.g., oil analysis, brake measurements)
Use telematics/fault trends to anticipate failures
Deliberately allow failure on low-impact items
Only acceptable for non-critical, low-cost items

callout.title: A plan is a set of choices
callout.text: Strong fleets mix strategies: intervals for fluids and inspections, condition-based for brakes and tires, predictive for aftertreatment and engines using fault data. Safety-critical systems are never run-to-failure.

body.title: Choosing a strategy by consequence and predictability

example.title: Brake measurements instead of fixed intervals
example.text: A fleet replaced brake linings every set interval regardless of wear. By measuring lining thickness and pushrod stroke at each PM (condition-based), they replaced only worn components and caught fast-wearing units earlier — lowering cost and reducing brake-related out-of-service events.

exercise.prompt: Choose the most suitable strategy for each item.

items.text: Engine oil and filters
items.why: Classic interval item (sometimes extended with oil analysis).

items.text: Brake linings on a mixed-duty fleet
items.why: Wear varies by duty — measure and replace when needed.

items.text: Aftertreatment faults trending across the fleet
items.why: Fault-code trends can predict failures before derates.

items.text: Annual inspection

check.q: Which is never acceptable for safety-critical systems?
check.e: Safety-critical components must not be allowed to fail in service.

check.q: Availability is reduced by planned maintenance as well as breakdowns.
check.e: Any time a unit can't work reduces availability — which is why PM timing matters.

takeaways: Balance reliability, availability and cost.
Mix interval, condition-based and predictive strategies.
Never run safety-critical items to failure.
Plan PMs to minimize availability impact.
tips: Write down which strategy applies to each major system — then check the PM program matches.
Use failure data to move items from "unpredictable" to "predictable".
mistakes: Applying one interval to everything.
Letting a safety item drift into run-to-failure by neglect.

deep.title: Continuous improvement

items.d: Change a PM task or interval

blocks: PDCA keeps a maintenance program honest: every change is a small experiment that's measured before it becomes the standard.

objectives: Identify failure trends across the fleet
body: Failure trends reveal systemic issues: a component that fails across a model year, a vendor whose repairs don't hold, a route that destroys tires.

Maintenance cost per mile generally rises as equipment ages, while the value of the vehicle falls. At some point, keeping an aging unit costs more — in repairs, downtime and reliability — than replacing it.

ul: Accurate cost and downtime history per unit
Repeat-failure and major-component failure records
Early warning on units with rising CPM
Input on which specs/configurations perform best

callout.title: Data wins replacement debates
callout.text: Replacement decisions are made by fleet leadership and finance. The coordinator's clean data — CPM trends, downtime, major repairs — is what makes those decisions sound.

body.title: From data to a replacement decision

example.title: The expensive old unit
example.text: T-101 (8 years, 890,000 miles) had $31,000 in maintenance last year and 41 days of downtime. Newer units averaged $11,000 and 6 days. The coordinator's report — with costs, downtime and upcoming major repairs — helped leadership move T-101 up the replacement schedule.

exercise.prompt: Five units of the same model year all had EGR cooler failures between 380,000 and 420,000 miles. Eight other units of that model are at 330,000–370,000 miles. What should you recommend?

options.text: Wait for each to fail and repair on the roadside
options.why: Predictable failures handled reactively cost more and risk engine damage.

options.text: Share the trend with the fleet manager, check warranty/manufacturer bulletins, and plan inspections on the at-risk units at their next PMs
options.why: Uses the trend to prevent failures and recover costs.

options.text: Replace the EGR coolers on all eight immediately without review
options.why: Premature — inspect and verify, check warranty and bulletins first.

check.q: As a vehicle ages, maintenance cost per mile typically:
check.e: Older equipment generally costs more to maintain.

check.q: Coordinators typically make the final vehicle replacement decision alone.
check.e: Leadership and finance decide; coordinators supply the data.

takeaways: Look for failure trends by model, component, vendor and route.
Lifecycle: rising maintenance cost vs falling value.
Clean cost and downtime data drive replacement decisions.
Use trends to act before predictable failures.
tips: Flag units whose CPM is rising faster than the fleet average.
List known upcoming major repairs — they change the replacement math.
mistakes: Arguing replacement with opinions instead of cost and downtime data.
Ignoring downtime when comparing old and new units.

blocks.title: A vehicle's life in the fleet

objectives: Break a maintenance budget into its main categories
Build a simple forecast from miles and cost per mile
Explain budget variance and what drives it
body: At the expert level you are expected to explain where maintenance money goes and what next quarter will cost. A budget is a plan; a forecast updates the plan with what is actually happening.

body.title: Where an annual maintenance budget goes (example fleet)
body.note: Illustrative split. Actual budgets vary with fleet age, duty cycle and whether shops are in-house.

body.title: Budget vs. actual by month (example)
body.note: February's overrun came from two unplanned engine repairs — exactly the kind of item that belongs in an explanation, not just a number.

example.title: Explaining a variance
example.text: Maintenance ran 14% over budget in February. Instead of just reporting the number, the coordinator showed that two engine repairs ($11,800) caused the overrun, that one was a warranty claim in progress, and that CPM without those two events was 3% under plan. Leadership approved the variance in one meeting.

exercise.source:
Planned miles: 1,500,000
Fleet cost per mile (trailing 12 months): $0.12
Known major repairs: 2 clutches at $4,800 each
Quarter budget: $190,000

check.q: A forecast differs from a budget because it:
o: Updates the plan with actual results and known upcoming events
check.e: Forecasts are living estimates; budgets are the plan.

check.q: Budget $56,000, actual $63,900. Variance %?

takeaways: Know your budget categories and their shares.
Forecast = planned miles × CPM + known major repairs.
Always explain variances with causes, not just numbers.
Separate one-off events from trend changes.
tips: Keep a running list of known upcoming major repairs.
Report variance with a one-line cause for each large item.
mistakes: Reporting variance numbers without explanations.
Forecasting from last year's total when miles changed.

objectives: Interpret what each KPI tells you

head: KPI
Formula
What it tells you
rows: Efficiency of spend, comparable across units
Average spend per unit over a period
Share of time units are unavailable
PMs completed on time ÷ PMs due × 100

callout.title: Define before you measure
callout.text: Decide exactly what counts: Does downtime include PMs? What window defines a "repeat" (e.g., same system within 30 days)? What counts as "on time" for a PM? Inconsistent definitions make KPIs meaningless.

example.title: Downtime percentage
example.text: A 50-unit fleet over 30 days has 50 × 720 = 36,000 available hours. Units were down a combined 1,440 hours. Downtime % = 1,440 ÷ 36,000 = 4.0%. Availability = 96.0%.

exercise.source:
Maintenance cost: $62,000
Miles driven: 480,000
PMs due: 36   PMs done on time: 33
Total repairs: 90   Repeat repairs (same system ≤30 days): 9
Road calls: 12

check.q: PM compliance is calculated as:
o: PMs completed on time ÷ PMs due × 100
check.e: On-time PMs as a share of PMs due.

check.q: Why must a "repeat repair" be clearly defined?
o: Without a consistent definition, the KPI can't be compared over time
check.e: Consistent definitions make KPIs trustworthy.

takeaways: Know the formulas: CPM, cost per vehicle, downtime %, PM compliance, repeat rate, breakdown frequency.
Each KPI answers a different question.
Define terms before measuring.
Compare trends over time, not single points.
tips: Publish your KPI definitions so everyone measures the same way.
Show trends over at least 3–6 periods.
mistakes: Changing a definition mid-year and comparing the numbers anyway.
Reporting a KPI without the action it suggests.

blocks.title: PM compliance % by terminal and month
blocks.note: Memphis is sliding while Phoenix improves — ask what changed at each terminal.

objectives: Use a KPI dashboard to find problems

tiles.title: MTBF
tiles.text: Mean Time Between Failures = operating time ÷ number of failures. Higher is better.

tiles.title: MTTR
tiles.text: Mean Time To Repair = total repair (downtime) hours ÷ number of repairs. Lower is better.

tiles.title: Vendor performance
tiles.text: Turnaround time, cost vs estimate, comeback rate, communication — per vendor.

example.title: MTBF vs MTTR
example.text: A fleet improved MTBF from 3,100 to 3,900 operating hours by fixing a recurring aftertreatment issue — fewer failures. Separately, MTTR fell from 26 to 18 hours after approvals were moved to a 24/7 on-call process — faster repairs. Two different problems, two different fixes.

exercise.prompt: Which KPI does each improvement most directly affect?

items.text: Pre-approving common repairs up to a limit
Eliminating a recurring sensor failure
items.why: Fewer failures = longer time between them.

items.text: Scheduling PMs during driver home time
Stocking common parts at terminal shops

check.q: A fleet logged 60,000 operating hours with 20 failures. MTBF is:
20 repairs took a total of 400 downtime hours. MTTR is:

takeaways: MTBF measures reliability; MTTR measures repair speed.
Availability combines them into "ready to work" time.
Vendor performance needs multiple measures.
Different problems need different fixes — the metrics tell you which.

objectives: Distinguish symptom, failure and root cause
Gather the right data for analysis

head: Level
Definition
Example
rows: Why it failed — the underlying reason that, if fixed, prevents recurrence
Wrong coolant mix causing seal degradation

body: Fixing the failure returns the truck to service. Fixing the root cause keeps it — and the rest of the fleet — from failing again.
Ask "why?" repeatedly until you reach a cause you can act on. It's simple, but powerful when grounded in evidence — not assumptions.

timeline.title: Why did the water pump leak?
Why did the seal fail early?
timeline.text: Coolant tests showed contamination and incorrect mixture.

timeline.title: Why was the coolant incorrect?
timeline.text: Top-offs used whatever coolant was available on the road.

timeline.title: Why were mixed coolants used?
timeline.text: Drivers had no approved coolant or guidance. → Root cause: no top-off standard. Fix: approved coolant in trucks + driver guidance + coolant testing at PM.

ul: Repair history (dates, mileage, parts, vendors)
Driver reports and DVIRs
Parts failure records and returned parts
Maintenance trends across similar units
Fault code history from telematics

body.title: Cause-and-effect (fishbone): why does T-120 keep derating?

causes: Different diagnostic tools at each vendor

body.note: A fishbone diagram organizes possible causes by category before you test them. Evidence decides which ones are real.

body.title: Symptom → failure → root cause (example)

items.t: Root cause: worn tensioner never checked at PM

body.note: Replacing the alternator fixes the failure. Adding the tensioner to the PM checklist fixes the root cause — and stops the repeat.

body.title: The 5 Whys on the same case
body.note: Illustrative chain. Stop asking "why" when you reach something you can change in a process — not when you reach a part.

example.title: Three turbos in a year
example.text: A unit went through three turbochargers. Each shop replaced the turbo — fixing the failure. RCA found an oil supply restriction starving the turbo. Fixing the oil line stopped the failures.

exercise.prompt: Arrange this chain from symptom to root cause.
items: Irregular wear on inside edges of one axle
Alignment not checked after suspension repair
No post-repair alignment check in procedure

check.q: Which statement is a root cause rather than a failure?
o: Belt tensioner not included in PM inspection checklist
check.e: A missing inspection step explains why failures occur — fixing it prevents recurrence.

check.q: Replacing the failed part always eliminates the root cause.
check.e: Replacing the part fixes the failure; the underlying reason may remain.

takeaways: Symptom → failure → root cause.
Fixing the root cause prevents recurrence.
Use 5 Whys grounded in evidence.
Combine repair history, driver reports, parts data and trends.
tips: Collect evidence for each "why" — photos, data, returned parts.
Involve the technician and driver in the analysis.
mistakes: Stopping at the failed part.
Blaming a person when the process allowed the failure.

objectives: Conduct an RCA using repair history
body: T-120 has had repeated aftertreatment problems. Review the history.

accordion.title: Pattern
accordion.text: Three derates in about 60 days, ~7,000 miles apart. Each repair addressed the immediate failure (a loaded DPF) but not why the DPF kept loading.

accordion.title: Contributing factors
accordion.text: High idle time reduces exhaust temperatures, limiting passive regeneration. Clearing codes without finding the cause. A failing sensor may have been present since April. Three different vendors meant no one saw the whole history.

accordion.title: Probable root cause
accordion.text: A combination: a failing sensor preventing successful regens, aggravated by heavy idling. Confirmed by the dealer's sensor finding and the idle data.

accordion.title: Corrective actions
accordion.text: Verify repair holds (monitor regen data). Address idling with operations/driver guidance. Share full history with vendors. Check warranty on the April/May work. Review other units with similar idle profiles.

callout.title: Send the history with the truck
callout.text: Many repeat failures persist because each shop sees only today's complaint. Include relevant history in every repair request.

example.title: Result
example.text: After the sensor replacement and an idle-reduction plan, T-120 ran four months without an aftertreatment event. The fleet also added a rule: any unit with two derates in 60 days triggers an RCA review.

exercise.prompt: Which corrective actions address root causes for T-120? (Select all that apply)

options.text: Clear the codes whenever the lamp comes on
Work with operations to reduce excessive idling
Include full repair history with every repair request
options.why: Prevents shops from repeating incomplete repairs.

options.text: Create an RCA trigger: 2 derates in 60 days
options.why: A systemic control for future repeats.

options.text: Switch to a new vendor each time
options.why: Fragmenting history makes repeats more likely.

check.q: Why did T-120's repairs keep failing?
o: Each repair treated the immediate failure, not the underlying causes
check.e: Without addressing why the DPF loaded, it kept loading.

check.q: A shop wants to clear codes and release the truck for a third derate in 60 days. You:
o: Ask for root-cause diagnosis, share the full history, and check warranty on recent repairs
Send it to a different shop without history
check.e: Break the cycle with diagnosis and history.

takeaways: Repair history reveals patterns individual repairs miss.
Look for contributing factors, not just a single part.
Share history with every vendor.
Create triggers that start RCA automatically.
tips: Plot repeat failures on a mileage line — the spacing tells a story.
Send the full history with the unit to the next shop.
mistakes: Switching vendors each time and losing the history.
Treating each repeat as a new, unrelated case.

deep.title: Pareto: focus on the vital few

blocks.title: Road calls by cause — last 12 months
blocks.note: The top three causes account for about 80% of road calls (99 of 125) — the classic Pareto (80/20) pattern. Start RCA there.

objectives: Break a complex breakdown into workstreams
body: Complex breakdowns — loaded truck, deadline, parts shortage, dispatch pressure — overwhelm people who handle them one call at a time. Experts run parallel workstreams.

tiles.title: 1. Safety
tiles.text: Driver and vehicle secure. Safety-critical defects identified. Non-negotiable first step.

tiles.title: 2. Repair
tiles.text: Vendor, diagnosis, parts, ETR. The "fix the truck" track.

tiles.title: 3. Load
tiles.text: Protect the freight: recovery, swap, reschedule — with dispatch.

tiles.title: 4. People
tiles.text: Driver care (food, hotel, HOS), customer communication via ops.

tiles.title: 6. Record
tiles.text: A running time-stamped log of everything.

callout.title: Decide the next decision
callout.text: At any moment, ask: What is the next decision, who makes it, and what information do they need? Then get that information.

body: During complex events, set a predictable update rhythm (e.g., every 60 minutes or at each milestone) so stakeholders stop calling you for status and you can work.

body.title: Workstreams run at the same time (first 3 hours)
body.note: Illustrative timing. Safety comes first; after that, nothing waits for anything else unless it has to.

example.title: The 5-minute plan
example.text: On a brake failure with a loaded reefer and a 10:00 delivery: Safety — driver off roadway, triangles out. Repair — mobile brake tech ETA 50 min. Load — dispatch checking for a recovery tractor as backup. People — driver has food; HOS checked. Cost — estimate will be routed immediately. Record — case log started. Update cadence set: every 45 minutes.

exercise.prompt: Which workstream does each action belong to?

items.text: Confirm warning triangles are placed
Ask the dealer for parts availability
Ask dispatch for a recovery tractor option
Book a hotel for the driver near the shop

check.q: Which workstream always comes first?
check.e: Safety first, always.

check.q: Setting an update cadence reduces interruptions during complex events.
check.e: Predictable updates reduce status calls.

takeaways: Run six workstreams: safety, repair, load, people, cost, record.
Always ask: what is the next decision?
Set an update cadence.
Log everything as it happens.
tips: Say the workstreams out loud at the start: it stops you from tunnel vision.
Set the update cadence in your first message to stakeholders.
mistakes: Solving the repair perfectly while the load misses its window.
Taking status calls instead of working the next decision.

objectives: Coordinate a tractor breakdown during a load
Handle a parts shortage and shop availability problem
body: Work through the decision tree below. Your choices determine the outcome. Replay it to explore different paths.

callout.title: What experts optimize
callout.text: Not "the fastest repair" — the best overall outcome: safe, load protected, cost reasonable, stakeholders informed, and nothing lost in documentation.

body.title: How a complex breakdown unfolds

items.d: Mobile tech or tow to a shop

body.note: Expect each stage to change your plan. Re-check safety and the ETR every time it does.

example.title: Why paths diverge
example.text: Two coordinators faced the same breakdown. One focused only on the repair and waited on a part for 2 days — the load missed its deadline. The other started a recovery plan in parallel; when the part delay was confirmed, a swap was ready within the hour.

ul: Which decision had the largest impact on the outcome?
At what point should the recovery plan have started?
What information did dispatch need, and when?

check.q: The only nearby shop can't start for 2 days; the part is also 2 days out. The load is due tomorrow. What first?
o: Start the recovery plan with dispatch now while sourcing faster repair options
Tell the driver to keep driving
check.e: Parallel workstreams: protect the load while pursuing the repair.

check.q: Dispatch pushes to run a truck with a brake defect "just 40 miles." Correct response?
o: Decline, explain it's a safety-critical defect, and offer the fastest safe alternatives
check.e: Short distance doesn't change a safety-critical defect.

takeaways: Start recovery planning early when ETR confidence is low.
Safety-critical defects are never negotiable.
Parallel workstreams create options.
Optimize the overall outcome, not one variable.

head: Criterion
How to measure
rows: Average hours from arrival to release
Average invoice vs estimate; labor rate; fees
Repeat repairs attributable to the vendor
Diagnosis on time, proactive updates, clear estimates
How quickly they can start; after-hours support

body: Weights reflect priorities. A time-sensitive fleet might weight repair time heavily; a cost-focused fleet might weight cost. Adjust the weights below and watch the ranking change.

example.title: Fast but costly
example.text: Vendor A is the fastest but 15% more expensive. Vendor B is cheapest but has a 12% comeback rate. With quality weighted properly, Vendor A often wins overall — because comebacks create second downtime events.

ul: Set Quality to the highest weight — which vendor leads?
Set Cost to the highest weight — does the leader change?
Which vendor is consistently strong regardless of weights?

check.q: Comeback rate primarily measures:
check.e: Comebacks mean the repair didn't fix the problem.

check.q: Scorecard weights should reflect the fleet's priorities.
check.e: Weights encode what matters most to the operation.

takeaways: Measure time, cost, quality, repeats, communication, availability, coverage.
Weight criteria by fleet priorities.
Cheapest is rarely best when quality is weak.
Use data, not impressions.

body: Vendors are partners. The best relationships combine clear expectations, prompt payment and honest feedback.

timeline.title: Set expectations
timeline.text: Communication times, approval rules, documentation (complaint/cause/correction), invoice format.

timeline.title: Review
timeline.text: Share results periodically — good and bad.

timeline.title: Address issues
timeline.text: Specific examples, requested corrective action, follow-up date.

timeline.title: Decide
timeline.text: Preferred, standard, or not used — per company policy.

msg.title: Performance conversation — to shop manager
msg.text: Hi Dana — appreciate the quick turnarounds this quarter. One concern: 3 of our last 9 repairs at your shop came back within 30 days (T-120, T-126, TR-540). Can we review those together this week and agree on steps to prevent repeats? I'll send the case details beforehand.

body.title: Addressing vendor performance, step by step

levels.d: Specific case, specific issue, same week.
Share the data: comebacks, response time, cost.
Agreed actions and a review date.

body.note: Climb only as far as you need. Most issues are fixed at the first or second step when the data is clear.

example.title: Turning a vendor around
example.text: A shop with poor communication was asked to send diagnoses by a set time and use a standard estimate format. Within two months its communication score rose from the bottom to the top third.

exercise.prompt: A vendor has overbilled twice this month. Best first message?

options.text: "Two invoices this month exceeded the approved estimates without authorization (RO 8812: +$640; RO 8840: +$310). Please review and issue corrections, and let's confirm the approval process going forward."
options.why: Specific, factual and focused on correction.
Rewards the behavior and loses money.

check.q: The most effective performance feedback is:
o: Specific, factual and with a requested action
check.e: Specifics and actions lead to change.

check.q: Sharing positive feedback with vendors is part of good vendor management.
check.e: Recognition reinforces what you want more of.

takeaways: Set expectations, measure, review, address, decide.
Feedback: specific, factual, action-oriented.
Recognize good performance too.
Preferred networks are built on data and trust.

objectives: Know what information a claim needs

head: Type
Covers
Check

Engines, transmissions, aftertreatment, etc. — may differ from base
Repairs done by a shop — often months/miles

callout.text: Repeat repairs within a shop's parts/labor warranty, or component failures within manufacturer coverage, are commonly paid by the fleet simply because nobody checked.

In-service date and current mileage/hours

body.title: Overlapping warranty windows (example terms)
body.note: Illustrative terms only — real coverage depends on the manufacturer, contract, mileage and conditions. At month 30 the base warranty has expired, but the shop's repair warranty may still apply.

body.title: Is this repair a warranty claim?

items.d: Base, extended, parts or repair warranty
With the dealer or warranty provider
At a facility that can file the claim

body.note: Checking before work starts is the step that matters — many claims can't be recovered after a non-authorized shop does the repair.

body.title: Common types of coverage
head: Type
What it usually covers
Where to check
rows: Components of a new vehicle for a set time or mileage
Specific systems beyond the base warranty
A replacement part that fails early
The labor on a previous repair
body.note: Terms vary by manufacturer and contract — always read the actual coverage documents.

example.title: The 11-month turbo
example.text: A turbo failed 11 months after an independent shop replaced it. The shop's parts warranty was 12 months. Because the coordinator checked history before approving, the shop replaced it at no parts cost.

exercise.prompt: Should you investigate warranty before approving?

items.text: Starter failed 4 months after replacement at Shop B
items.why: Recent repair — likely within parts/labor warranty.

items.text: New tractor, 30,000 miles, transmission fault
Tire destroyed by road debris
items.why: Road hazard damage — not a defect (unless a road hazard policy exists).

items.text: Water pump replaced 14 months ago by a dealer
items.why: Some parts carry longer warranties — worth checking.

check.q: When is the best time to identify warranty?
check.e: Early identification preserves the claim and may require specific facilities.

check.q: Maintenance records can be requested as part of a warranty claim.
check.e: Warrantors may request proof of proper maintenance.

takeaways: Know base, component, extended and repair warranties.
Check history before approving repairs.
Claims need VIN, serials, mileage, ROs and failure details.
Unchecked warranty is lost money.
tips: Keep in-service dates and component serials on file for every unit.
Make warranty a checkbox on every repair over a set amount.
mistakes: Checking only the base vehicle warranty.
Letting a shop discard a failed part that a claim needs.

objectives: Communicate a warranty claim to a vendor

msg.title: Warranty request to shop
msg.text: Hi Mike — T-126 is back with a no-start. Your RO 7731 (02/14, 388,400 mi) replaced the starter. Current mileage 402,100 — about 4 months and 13,700 miles later. Please diagnose under your parts/labor warranty and confirm coverage before additional repairs. RO copy attached.

body: Document: the claim, the reference (original RO), what was covered (parts, labor, both), what the fleet paid, and the final outcome. Track warranty recovery as a KPI — it shows the value of disciplined history checks.

callout.title: Keep failed parts when asked
callout.text: Warranty claims may require the failed part. Tell shops up front not to discard parts when a claim is possible.

body.title: What a warranty claim packet contains
rows: Factual complaint and when it started
Invoice for the earlier part or repair, if any
body.note: Missing items are the most common reason claims stall. Build the packet as the repair happens, not after.

example.title: Recovery adds up
example.text: A 60-unit fleet started logging warranty checks on every repair over $500. In six months, recovered claims totaled $18,400 — money that previously went unclaimed.

exercise.source:
Prior RO 7731 — Shop: Mike's Diesel — 02/14 — 388,400 mi — Starter replaced (new) — 12 mo / unlimited mi parts & labor
Current — 06/18 — 402,100 mi — No-start, starter suspected

check.q: A warranty request to a shop should reference:
o: The original RO, dates, mileage and current complaint
check.e: Specific references make claims easy to verify.

check.q: Tracking warranty recovery as a KPI demonstrates the value of history checks.
check.e: Recovered dollars are a measurable outcome.

takeaways: Reference original RO, dates and mileage.
Confirm coverage before extra work.
Keep failed parts when required.
Track warranty recovery as a KPI.

objectives: Know when and how to escalate

ul: Safety concerns not being resolved
Costs above your approval authority
Downtime threatening customer commitments
Vendor disputes you can't resolve
Repeat failures needing policy or budget decisions
Conflicts between departments

head: Part
Content
rows: What is happening now, in one sentence
Your analysis of the risk and options
What you propose and what you need from them

msg.title: Escalation to fleet manager
msg.text:
S: T-120 down again — third aftertreatment derate in 60 days.
B: Prior repairs 04/02, 04/28, 05/30 at three vendors. Dealer found failed sensor 05/30.
A: Likely unresolved root cause plus heavy idling. Warranty may cover the 05/30 work.
R: Approve dealer diagnosis today ($450) with full history; I'll open a warranty claim and propose an idle-reduction plan with ops. Need approval by 11:00 to hold the dealer slot.

body: Stay factual, acknowledge the other person's pressure, state what you can and cannot do, and offer options. Customers are normally handled by operations or customer service — coordinate through them unless your company assigns you that role.

body.title: The escalation ladder

levels.d: Within your approval limit and written procedure.
Capacity conflicts, unclear procedure, disputes with dispatch.
Costs above your limit, repeat failures, vendor disputes.
Major customer impact, policy or budget decisions.

body.note: Safety or compliance concerns go to the safety department immediately — at any level, without climbing the ladder first.

body.title: SBAR — escalate in four parts
body.note: Example: "T-127 is down loaded in Amarillo (S). Brake repair needs a part arriving tomorrow (B). We'll miss the 13:00 delivery (A). I recommend a power swap from T-140 — approve the deadhead? (R)"

example.title: Saying no to a VP
example.text: A senior manager asked to release a truck with an unrepaired brake defect for a key customer. The coordinator acknowledged the customer importance, explained the defect was safety-critical, and presented two alternatives: a recovery tractor in 90 minutes or a mobile brake repair in 2 hours. The manager chose the recovery tractor.

exercise.prompt: Place each sentence in the SBAR structure.

items.text: Five units are down this morning, two with loads due today.
Our main shop lost two technicians last week.
Without added capacity, we'll miss both deliveries.
Approve overflow to Dealer C today at a higher rate.

check.q: What does the "R" in SBAR ask for?
o: Your recommendation and what you need
check.e: End with a clear recommendation and request.

check.q: A senior manager's request overrides a safety-critical defect.
check.e: Safety is non-negotiable regardless of seniority — offer safe alternatives.

takeaways: Escalate safety, authority, customer, vendor and policy issues.
Use SBAR for clear escalation.
In difficult conversations: facts, empathy, limits, options.
Safety is never negotiable — at any level.
tips: Escalate with SBAR and a deadline for the decision.
Bring options, not only the problem.
mistakes: Escalating late to avoid looking weak.
Escalating without a recommendation.

body: Work through these scenarios. Each response has consequences — read the reasoning after you choose.

example.title: Leading without authority
example.text: Coordinators rarely manage the people they depend on. Influence comes from reliability: accurate ETRs, clear messages, follow-through. Over time, dispatch and shops trust your information — and your recommendations carry weight.

ul: Do I lead escalations with the ask?
Do I present options, not just problems?
Do I follow up on commitments I make?

check.q: Where does a coordinator's influence mainly come from?
check.e: Trust is built by consistent, accurate communication.

check.q: When bringing a problem to management, you should also bring:
check.e: Options and recommendations make decisions faster.

takeaways: Bring options and a recommendation.
Stay calm and factual under pressure.
Follow through builds influence.
Choose the right audience and channel.

msg.title: DESC example — to a dispatcher
msg.text:
D: Twice this week units were released from the shop and sat 3+ hours waiting for a driver.
E: That adds downtime and our availability KPI suffers for work that's already done.
S: Can we agree that I send you the ETR 2 hours ahead and you assign pickup then?
C: Trucks roll sooner — and you get more capacity back each day.

body: Disruptions — storms, a cold snap, a bad fuel batch, a shop closure — can put many units down at once. The principles scale: safety, triage, capacity, communication.

ol: Life safety — drivers in danger, vehicles in unsafe locations
Safety-critical defects — brakes, steering, tires, lighting, fire risk
Revenue impact — loaded units, then empty units

body: When shop capacity is limited, allocate slots to units with the highest combined safety and operational impact. Use mobile service for jobs that don't need a bay. Consider overflow vendors at a higher rate when downtime cost justifies it.

callout.title: Driver constraints
callout.text: In a disruption, drivers may run out of hours, need lodging, or be stuck in dangerous weather. Driver safety and welfare remain priorities — coordinate with dispatch and safety.

body: Set up a single status list, update leadership on a fixed cadence, and give dispatch one consolidated picture instead of dozens of individual calls.

levels.d: People in danger, vehicles in unsafe locations.
Brakes, steering, tires, lighting, fire risk.
Reefer loads, hard deadlines, high-value freight.
Loaded units first, then empty units.

body.title: Disruption board at 07:00 (illustrative)
head: Unit
Situation
Priority
Next action
rows: Shoulder of I-40, no-start, driver in cab
Driver safety check; warning devices; mobile tech
Reefer alarm, pharma load, temp rising slowly

body.note: Order follows the triage pyramid: people, safety defects, time-critical cargo, revenue, then routine work.

body.title: Communication rhythm during a disruption

items.d: Board shared with dispatch and leadership
Summary and open items handed over

body.note: A predictable rhythm cuts interruptions — people stop calling when they know when the next update comes.

example.title: Cold snap morning
example.text: At −15°F, nine units reported no-starts and gelled fuel. The coordinator triaged: two units with drivers in unsafe roadside locations first, then a reefer load, then loaded units at customers. Mobile services handled fuel-related starts; three units were towed. Leadership got a consolidated update every hour.

items: Driver stranded on a highway shoulder in a storm, truck won't start
Loaded unit with brake air leak at a truck stop
Reefer with failing unit and temperature-sensitive cargo
Loaded dry van with amber check engine light, driving normally
Empty trailer at the yard with a door latch issue

check.q: With limited shop capacity, which unit should get the first bay?
o: The unit with the highest combined safety and operational impact
check.e: Allocate scarce capacity by impact.

check.q: During disruptions, a single consolidated status list helps dispatch and leadership.
check.e: One source of truth reduces confusion.

takeaways: Triage: life safety, safety-critical, time-critical, revenue, routine.
Allocate scarce capacity by impact.
Use mobile and overflow vendors strategically.
One status list, fixed update cadence.
tips: Build one status list and share it — don't run a disruption from memory.
Pre-arrange overflow vendors before storm season.
mistakes: Triaging by who called first.
Sending leadership raw message threads.

objectives: Apply triage to a live board
body: Classify each unit and then choose the consolidated update for leadership.

example.title: What leadership needs
example.text: Leadership doesn't need every detail. They need: how many units are down, how many loads are at risk, what you're doing, what you need from them, and when the next update comes.

exercise.prompt: Which leadership update is best during a disruption?

options.why: Leadership can't extract decisions from raw threads.

options.text: "07:00 update — 9 units down (7% of fleet). 2 drivers in unsafe locations: tows en route, ETA 30 min. 1 reefer at risk: mobile reefer tech ETA 45 min. 4 loaded units: 2 recovered by swaps, 2 late (ops notifying customers). Need: approval for overflow shop at +$25/h. Next update 08:00."
options.why: Numbers, safety, risks, actions, ask, cadence.

options.text: "It's bad out there, we're handling it."

check.q: A leadership update during a disruption should include:
o: Units down, safety issues, loads at risk, actions, asks, next update
check.e: Decision-ready summaries.

check.q: Empty trailers with minor issues should be prioritized over drivers in unsafe locations.
check.e: Life safety always comes first.

takeaways: Life safety first, always.
Consolidate information for leadership.
Use numbers, actions and asks.
Keep a fixed update cadence.

blocks.title: Units down by hour — cold snap morning
blocks.note: The peak was 07:00. Knowing the curve helps plan overflow vendors and leadership updates.

objectives: Separate what happened from why it happened
Turn lessons into specific process changes
body: When a disruption ends, the pressure drops — and so does attention. Expert coordinators use that moment to capture lessons before they are forgotten. An after-action review (AAR) is a short, blame-free debrief focused on improving the process.

body.title: AAR summary template
rows: Winter PM with fuel additive and battery tests completed by 12/01
4 units missed winter PM; 6 gelled-fuel no-starts
PM slots lost to a shop closure in November; no escalation
Triage by life safety; hourly leadership updates
Winter-prep tracker with weekly review — Owner: J. Taylor · Due 10/15

callout.title: Blame-free, not accountability-free
callout.text: AARs look at process and decisions, not personalities. Each action item still gets a named owner and a due date.

example.title: One change, fewer road calls
example.text: After a cold-snap AAR, a fleet created a winter-prep tracker and moved battery testing into the fall PM. The next winter, fuel- and battery-related road calls fell by more than half.

exercise.prompt: Which AAR action item is best written?

options.why: Not specific, no owner, no date — it won't change anything.

options.text: "Create a winter-prep tracker covering battery tests and fuel treatment for all units, reviewed weekly from 10/01. Owner: J. Taylor. Due: 10/15."

check.q: The main goal of an after-action review is to:
o: Improve the process for next time
check.e: AARs turn experience into better processes.

check.q: Every AAR action item should have an owner and a due date.
check.e: Without ownership, lessons stay on paper.

takeaways: Run AARs soon after the event, while memory is fresh.
Four questions: planned, happened, why, what changes.
Keep it blame-free but give every action an owner and date.
Capture what worked well, too.
tips: Build the timeline from your case log before the meeting.
Keep AARs to 30 minutes with a written one-page summary.
mistakes: Skipping the AAR because "things are back to normal".
Action items with no owner.

objectives: Explain what telematics data a coordinator can use
Triage fault alerts without alert fatigue
Use remote diagnostics to route units to the right shop
body: [[Telematics]] turns every truck into a data source: location, fault codes, fuel, idle time, and more. Used well, it lets you act before the driver calls. Used badly, it buries you in alerts.

body.title: Alert tiering to prevent alert fatigue

levels.d: Stop-engine, low oil pressure, high coolant temp, air/brake faults.
Derate risk: aftertreatment, DEF, repeated active codes.
Codes that can be combined with the next PM or shop visit.
Inactive or one-time codes; trend them.

body.title: Active fault alerts by unit and week (example)
body.note: A rising row is a unit heading for a roadside failure. T-120's pattern justified a proactive dealer visit.

industry.name: Samsara
industry.text: Samsara offers a connected operations platform. Its website lists fleet capabilities including live GPS tracking, vehicle diagnostics, fuel analytics and compliance reporting, plus AI-powered dash cams and in-cab alerts for driver safety.
industry.relevance: Fault alerts, location and diagnostic data from a telematics platform are the inputs to the alert-tiering process in this lesson. Dash cams and in-cab alerts are part of the driver-safety side of the same technology.

example.title: Fixed before the call
example.text: At 04:10 telematics showed T-131 with an active coolant-level code and a slowly rising temperature. The coordinator messaged the driver at the next stop, confirmed a small leak, and booked a shop 20 miles ahead. The hose was replaced at 07:30 — no roadside event, no tow.

exercise.prompt: Assign each alert to a tier.

items.text: Low oil pressure warning, active, truck at highway speed
items.why: Engine damage risk — contact driver immediately.

items.text: DPF soot load high, regen requested, no derate yet
Inactive cab HVAC code, occurred once
Air pressure dropping with low-air warning

check.q: What is "alert fatigue"?
o: So many low-value alerts that important ones get missed
check.e: Tiering prevents critical alerts from drowning in noise.

check.q: A telematics fault code alone is enough to order parts.
check.e: Codes guide diagnosis; technicians confirm.

takeaways: Telematics lets you act before the driver calls.
Tier alerts: act now, act today, plan, watch.
Trends by unit reveal failures in progress.
Codes guide — technicians confirm.
tips: Agree on alert tiers with safety and dispatch.
Send the telematics snapshot to the shop with the unit.
mistakes: Turning on every alert and then ignoring them all.
Calling a driver while they're driving instead of at a safe stop.

objectives: Describe the role of a maintenance management system (CMMS)
Use leading indicators to drive decisions
body: Data only helps if it's complete, consistent and used. A maintenance management system ([[CMMS]]) — or fleet maintenance software — is where cases, work orders, PM schedules, parts and costs come together.

body.title: Data quality rules that pay off
head: Rule
Why
rows: Standard repair/system codes on every work order
PM, warranty and MTBF depend on it
Vendor and invoice linked to the case
Cost per vendor and dispute resolution
Time stamps for down and released

industry.name: Fleetio
industry.text: Fleetio is fleet management software. Its website describes it as "one place to run fleet maintenance," aimed at reducing downtime and controlling costs, for fleets in industries including trucking and freight.
industry.relevance: This is the category of system this lesson calls a CMMS. The data-quality rules above apply no matter which product a fleet uses.

example.title: Codes made the trend visible
example.text: A fleet had years of work orders with free-text notes like "fixed truck". After adding required system codes, one quarter of data showed that 38% of road calls were electrical — mostly corroded trailer connectors. A connector-sealing step at PM cut those road calls by more than half.

items.text: Units with PM overdue this week
Last month's road calls
Open safety defects from DVIRs
Quarterly maintenance cost per mile

check.q: Why require standard system codes on work orders?
o: To make trend analysis by system possible
check.e: Consistent codes turn records into usable data.

check.q: Which is a leading indicator?
check.e: PM compliance predicts future reliability.

takeaways: A CMMS brings cases, work orders, parts and costs together.
Data quality rules make analysis possible.
Use leading indicators to act early.
Close the loop: capture, clean, analyze, act, measure.
tips: Start with 5 data rules and enforce them — not 50.
Review one leading indicator in every weekly meeting.
mistakes: Free-text-only work orders.
Reporting lagging metrics without acting on leading ones.
